"A Los Angeles County lawmaker is pursuing legislation that would expand the use of electronic recording in state court proceedings, a proposal expected to draw heavy opposition from certified court reporters and their labor union.
Sen. Susan Rubio, D-Baldwin Park, has not made public specific bill language, and her office did not return messages seeking more information. But several legislative sources said the second-term state senator has told others in the Capitol that she intends to introduce legislation allowing electronic recording in civil and family law cases.
Jennafer Wagner, director of programs at the Family Violence Appellate Project, <https://www.sfpublicpress.org/california-could-allow-electronic-recording-in-civil-and-family-court-helping-poor-litigants/|told> the San Francisco Public Press on Feb. 20 that her organization is sponsoring the bill. In an email Wednesday, Wagner said she had “nothing to share at this time” on the proposed legislation.

Current law restricts electronic recording in state courts to limited civil, infraction and misdemeanor matters. Court reporters and their union, Service Employees International Union, a potent force in statehouse politics, have beaten back past legislative attempts to expand its use, arguing that the technology is unreliable and does not have the ability to pause proceedings if a party can’t be heard.
Rose Nava, a Los Angeles County court reporter, said Rubio’s bill would create a two-tiered system with parties who can afford to pay for private stenographers and parties who would have to rely instead on court-provided electronic reporting.
“Senator Rubio’s bill is wrong-headed and goes counter to current legislative priorities of ensuring courts have appropriate funding to recruit and retain court reporters who have always been considered the gold standard in capturing the verbatim record,” Nava said. “We believe all litigants are entitled to an accurate and quality transcript.”

Interest in electronic recording resurfaced in recent years as the COVID-19 pandemic increased remote hearings and technology and the numbers of certified court reporters across the state dropped. In November 2022, 54 trial court executive officers issued a <https://www.law.com/therecorder/2022/11/07/labor-union-judicial-leaders-draw-battle-lines-on-future-of-court-reporters/?utm_source=email&utm_medium=enl&utm_content=20221110&utm_campaign=lawbarometer&utm_term=law|press release> calling the shortage of court reporters a “crisis,” one that could not be solved with recently allocated funding from the state because “there is no one to hire.” The statement called for changes to “the current statutory framework” limiting the use of electronic recording.
That same month, the Judicial Council released a <https://www.law.com/therecorder/2022/11/28/report-calls-for-expansion-of-electronic-recording-and-court-recorder-recruitment/|report> recommending that the state increase its use of electronic reporting in cases where official reporters are not available.
Leading Democratic lawmakers, however, publicly <https://www.law.com/therecorder/2022/11/02/no-will-no-way-correcting-the-record-on-the-la-superior-court-reporter-shortage/|accused> Los Angeles County Superior Court specifically of not moving aggressively enough to retain and recruit official reporters. Then, in a striking turnabout, Los Angeles court executives earlier this month announced a new package of five-figure incentives to attract new official reporters and to lure veteran ones away from retirement.

“We are optimistic that these efforts … will help address the shortage,” court executive officer David Slayton said at the time.
Other state lawmakers have already introduced bills relating to court reporting and remote proceedings.
<https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB1214&search_keywords=%22court+reporters%22|AB 1214> by Assembly Judiciary Chairman Brian Maienschein would allow defendants, at their request, to appear remotely in all proceedings except for trials through 2026. Felony defendants could appear remotely at arraignments, initial court appearances and other limited instances that don’t involve testimony. The bill would also require the Judicial Council to set minimum technology standards for remote proceedings and it would bar courts from retaliating against court reporters who notify judges about remote connection troubles or sound problems.
<https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB22|SB 22> by Senate Judiciary Chairman Tom Umberg addresses some of the same issues as AB 1214 and would also extend until 2026 authority for courts to use remote proceedings in civil matters. Current statutory authority ends on July 1, 2023.
